subtopic: EXPULSION OF SOVIET OFFICIALS FROM CANADA

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXPULSION OF SOVIET OFFICIALS FROM CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to report on a matter of national security.
On the Government's instructions, a senior official of the Department of External Affairs informed the Soviet Ambassador on June 15 that seven Soviet officials were to leave Canada within 48 hours, and that one official, who was then outside Canada, would not be allowed to return to this country. Those seven officials left Canada on June 17. A further nine Soviet officials, who had already left Canada on completion of their assignments, were declared persona non grata and will not be permitted to return to Canada.
With the consent of the House, I will now table a list of the names of the Soviet officials concerned, and the Soviet establishments in Canada where each worked. I regret that the
only copy being tabled is in English. However, a French translation will be tabled immediately it is received by myself.
The Government acted after thorough investigations and analysis which led us to an inescapable conclusion that the Soviet officials concerned had engaged in unacceptable activities which were a threat to the security of this country. I do not intend to provide details of these activities except to say that some appeared designed to secure clandestine access to classified information or sensitive technology with commercial or military application.
Another operation was intended to penetrate the RCMP Security Service and, subsequently, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service. We are confident that Canadian security was not compromised.
Investigations are continuing in a number of the cases in question. I am confident that Canadian authorities have acted to preserve our security, and that the House would want me to express our appreciation to those authorities.
The 17 Soviet officials were not engaged in a single, large conspiracy, but several unrelated Soviet operations which were the subjects of parallel but distinct investigations. The investigations were complex and occurred over time.
Last Tuesday, the Government decided to take action on all the cases at once to bring them to an end.

Hon. Members may be aware of speculations about the Soviet citizen who was with the Secretariat of the International Civil Aviation Organization in Montreal.
I can now confirm that Mr. Yuriy Smurov has decided to apply for resident status in Canada, with his wife and daughter. His application is being examined by the Employment and Immigration Commission. I am advised that Mr. Smurov gave our security services useful information. However, I do not intend to elaborate on the kind of information provided.

Sir, we have impressed upon the Soviet authorities the seriousness with which we view the improper activities of Soviet officials and warned them against any resumption. The Canadian Government will not tolerate any activity by foreign powers which undermines the security or the sovereignty of our country.
At the same time, we indicated to the Soviet Union that we were prepared to put this matter behind us and get on with the

June 22, 1988

business of conducting our bilateral relations in accordance with our mutual interests.

subtopic: EXPULSION OF SOVIET OFFICIALS FROM CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) for his statement this afternoon. I must say that we on this side of the House had been expecting a statement for nearly five days, especially since in the past, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has tended to make such statements far more quickly.
Yesterday, at the end of the Fourteenth Economic Summit of G-7 countries in Toronto, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) confirmed that eight Soviets had been expelled for improper and unacceptable behaviour. We also heard that the eight had engaged in industrial espionage.
Today's statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, five days later, is of course welcome, and we thank him for it. However, there are still several question marks, although I realize that in the circumstances it may be difficult to reveal certain aspects of this matter.
In recent years, cases of industrial espionage have become increasingly frequent. Western advanced technology continues to attract industrial spies. In fact, the industrial espionage carries a high cost, not only for the industries and companies that are the target of such activities but also for the competitive position of a country like Canada.
Espionage, whether at the level of national security, at the level of industry, or at the level of scientific research, is reprehensible and deplorable. It strikes at the very heart and sovereignty of our country and leaves Canadians feeling helpless and vulnerable.
I recall that in 1978 the Hon. Don Jamieson, the then Secretary of State for External Affairs, rose in the House to reveal the details of a Soviet attempt to infiltrate the RCMP. At that time no risk was posed to our national security, and thanks to the alertness and effectiveness of the RCMP this Soviet espionage activity was nipped in the bud.
Today the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has revealed a few details of another disturbing espionage incident. Although we have obtained his reassurance that there was no threat to national security, we are nevertheless still extremely concerned about the impact that this may have, not only on our relations with the Soviet Union but also on the Canadian industries which will be the true victims of these deplorable actions by the Soviet Government. I would like to deal briefly with both those issues.

In the last few years, the Soviet Union has taken steps to reform both its domestic and foreign policy. East-West relations are becoming increasingly cordial, but we have to ask ourselves why the Soviet Union continues to threaten Canadian sovereignty by engaging in industrial espionage. One also wonders whether the Soviet Union is serious about its desire to improve relations with Canada.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs tells us that he sent a protest note to the Soviet government. I hope the Minister is willing to table the text of this diplomatic note in the House, as Minister Jamieson did in 1978, at the specific request of the Leader of the Opposition at the time, who today is the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I hope he will do what Mr. Jamieson did at the time.
The second point I referred to earlier concerns the victims of these breaches of security. I am sorry the Secretary of State for External Affairs did not bother to tell us whether the industries affected by this espionage were informed of the fact, but I hope the Government is considering ways to prevent any recurrence.

The timing of the announcement is, for us, something difficult to understand. Although the Secretary of State for External Affairs has not said anything about it, we suspect that there were probably consultations with the Americans or with other allies in this regard, wondering how Canada would cope with a possible retaliation that is normally the case when such action is taken by the Soviet Union. I hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is prepared to cope with this, without undermining at all the good reputation and position of Canada world-wide.

We are glad the Minister was able to say that Canada's security was not compromised. We regret, as does the Government, that this kind of unacceptable activity has been carried out by Soviet officials within Canada, putting Canadian security, sovereignty, and industry at risk.

Perhaps this is what the Minister had in mind when he said on behalf of the Government that he was prepared, to put this matter behind us and look forward to a new day when the spirit of perestroika and glasnost, the INF

subsubtopic: IN MEMORY OF JEAN ROCHON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Jean Rochon died yesterday. He dedicated his whole life to public affairs. He was first elected as Member of the Quebec Legislative Assembly in 1935, then as Member of the Parliament of Canada for Laval in 1962, 1963 and 1965 and for Ahuntsic in 1968. In 1972, when he could easily have been reelected, he graciously gave up his seat to help elect one of the first women Members from Quebec to Ottawa, Jeanne Sauve, who today is our gracious Governor General.
The people of Montreal, Laval and Ahuntsic wish to remember a good servant, Jean Rochon.

subtopic: S. O. 21 FORESTRY SPRUCE BUDWORM INFESTATION IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
S. O. 21 FORESTRY SPRUCE BUDWORM INFESTATION IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the Government's attention, especially to the attention of the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew), the extremely serious infestation by the spruce budworm in the forest lands of central British Columbia.
Within the Kamloops forest district alone, defoliation by the spruce budworm has exceeded 800,000 hectares, a doubling of the invaded area since 1986. Locations of the infestation include Heffley, Old Fadear Mill, Louis Creeks, Clearwater, Little Fort, Barriere, Adams Lake, Paul Lake, and Little Shuswap Lake areas, the Highland Valley, the Bonaparte Plateau, the Chase Region and many others. Recent Canadian forestry service reports indicate that an additional 600,000 hectares are under intensive budworm attack at this time.
This serious crisis is posing a major threat to the timber resource in central British Columbia and I urge the federal Government, through the Minister of State for Forestry, to initiate a special joint federal provincial emergency program immediately to combat this infestation in an effort to preserve these valuable timber lands and especially to maintain the thousands of jobs dependent upon this very important resource.

Mr. Speaker, a recent preliminary American trade ruling, once ratified, will have major benefits for Canadian hog producers. It is recommended that the existing American countervail duty on Canadian hogs be cut in half, going down 2.2 cents per pound from 4.39 cents per pound. This reduction will be retroactive to March, 1985.
This decision is of extreme importance to Manitoba hog producers. Manitoba exports a large number of hogs to the United States every year.
The preliminary ruling is also evidence of our need to continue to work toward establishing solid duty-free trade relationships for all of our commodities we trade with the United States. By establishing a good trading relationship, all of Canada will benefit from the solid economic gains free trade has to offer.
Manitoba hog producers know the benefits of free trade with the Americans. How can the Opposition suggest to them that export duties are good for their industry? Manitoba farmers do not believe in the Opposition's nonsense.

subsubtopic: REPORTED VIOLATIONS IN SINGAPORE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the human rights situation in Singapore is rapidly deteriorating, and the Canadian Government should be doing more than merely monitoring the situation.
Since 1984 there has been a noticeable decline in human rights in Singapore. For the first time in 20 years, in 1984 two opposition Members were elected to Parliament. Prime Minister Lee was said to have been disturbed by this development and is still upset that he does not control all the seats in Parliament.
Last May 22 people, mainly young church workers, students, lawyers and artists, were arrested for supposedly being involved in a Marxist conspiracy to overthrow the Government. Subsequently, international human rights groups rejected the charges as a pure fabrication stating that these individuals were merely exercising their civil rights within the law. After providing the Government with televised confessions of their involvement in this alleged conspiracy, all but one of them were released.
Eight of these people were recently rearrested by the Government after they stated that their confessions were false and were the product of long hours of interrogations and beatings. Once back in prison, however, the Government quickly succeeded in having the dissidents retract their stories of coercion and mistreatment, and they are still incarcerated.
Canada cannot sit idly by and watch the ongoing human rights abuses in Singapore, a state which is also a member of the Commonwealth.

subsubtopic: ROYAL BANK-FEE CHARGED FOR CREDIT RATING SEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today's bank special features the Royal Bank, Hanmer branch. My constituent, Marie June Ewen, had a loan at the branch and it was practically paid off this spring when she decided to renew the loan and increase it to pay her property taxes and insurance. She made that arrangement on May 9 and the bank deposited the amount into her account on May 11.
When she received her May bank statement, lo and behold, she noticed a service charge, $7 to register the loan, and $3. When she went to the bank to inquire about the $3, she found out from the manager of the bank that this was "the federal Government, by regulation, had asked for a credit rating search," and the bank was charging her $3 for the search.
This is another example of why we need an autonomous, independent ombudsman such as was recommended by members of this caucus.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR UNIFORM SYSTEM OF ADMISSIBILITY TO BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last weeks, I have received many requests about the variable eligibility weeks for unemployment insurance benefits.
The problem is the following: In my region, the unemployment level reaches 11.4 per cent. However, in some subregions, the level is above that. Now, the waiting period for the subregions is based on that of the region. Instead of having a waiting period in accordance with the subregion unemployment level, which is often higher, some people have to wait longer because of the lower unemployment level for the whole region. People living in these subregions are therefore penalized whenever their unemployment level is higher than the level for the region.
Because of this unfair situation, people generally feel dissatisfied.
The Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration prepared a report in which a specific solution to that unacceptable situation was recommended.
I therefore ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) to act on that recommendation so that a uniform system may be put in place which would not wrongfully penalized the citizens of this country, and especially my constituents.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: DESTRUCTION OF RAIN FORESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians join with environmentalists the world over to deplore the rapid depletion of the rain forests, especially the tropical rain forests so vital to the maintenance of existing patterns of wind and rain. At present rates of destruction there will be little left after the next five years. Yet it is we, in the cooler, non-tropical areas, who are likely to suffer the most from the climatic changes predicted with the loss of our global air conditioner.
We in the developed world are most responsible for this depletion in the name of progress and development. Canadians indeed help to finance this destruction through aid projects financed by the World Bank. We even give tax relief to Canadians living abroad to organize this slaughter in the name of development.
We live in a fragile, interdependent world. We must reassess our role in financing rain forest destruction. We must, with environmentalists everywhere, become part of the solution to this urgent global environmental problem. We must end our own complicity and work with others to protect the rain forests for our own sake and that of the whole world.

SAGUENAY-LAC-SAINT-JEAN 150 YEARS OF HISTORY-GREAT RALLY OF THE TREMBLAYS- TRIBUTE TO FOUNDERS

Mr. Speaker, the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region will be holding an important event this summer as we celebrate our first 150 years of history. All sorts of activities and events will be taking place throughout the summer. Among others, this week the Sague-nay-Lac-Saint-Jean will be hosting the great rally of the Tremblays which will coincide with our "fete des Quebecois" festivities on June 23, 24 and 25. Did you know, Mr. Speaker, that Tremblay is the surname of almost 15 percent of the people, some 45,000 in all, in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean area?
On the occasion of this 150th anniversary, Tremblays from all over the world will congregate to the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-
Jean to celebrate together our 150 years of history. Alexis Tremblay, familiarly known as "Picote", was one of the founders of our region. Some 150 years ago, Alexis Tremblay decided that the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean would be where his family would take root, and it did, Mr. Speaker!
In the name of all my colleagues here in the House, I would like to pay tribute to this great family on the occasion of its anniversary celebrations being held this week in Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean.

subsubtopic: HELSINKI ACID RAIN AGREEMENT-NON-SIGNATORIES BRITAIN AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, how could President Reagan and Prime Minister Thatcher agree to the Toronto Summit communique calling on strengthened international co-operation among all countries to protect the environment when the United States and Great Britain have not signed the Helsinki Protocol to cut acid rain-causing sulphur dioxide emissions? How could Reagan and Thatcher keep a straight face while agreeing to the Summit statement at a time when they are stalling negotiations in Geneva on another acid rain-causing pollutant, nitrous oxides?
Our natives speak of people with forked tongues. If Reagan and Thatcher do not speak with forked tongues, then they should practise what they preach by joining Canada, France, West Germany, Italy and 17 other nations in signing the Helsinki Agreement on Acid Rain. Next, they would instruct their negotiators in Geneva to reach an international agreement to control acid rain caused by nitrous oxides.
We heard statements on the environment from summits before. Neither Reagan nor Thatcher has so far showed any willingness to put their theory into practice. Will they this time?

RELEASE OF PENITENTIARY INMATE WITH HISTORY OF PSYCHIATRIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General. It involves the case of Joseph Roger Fredericks, who has a history of psychiatric problems dating back nearly 30 years. He also has a dangerous criminal record.
In November of 1984 he was convicted of gross sexual assault on an 11-year old Ottawa boy. He was sentenced to five years in penitentiary. He was released on day parole in November, 1987. In March of this year he was released on mandatory supervision.
In a letter to Mr. Fredericks dated November 16, 1986, the National Parole Board stated: "You have earned the support of the institution and the case management team. We believe the risks of releasing you are assumable".
On Monday Mr. Fredericks was charged with the first degree murder of an eleven-year old Brampton boy.
I would like the Solicitor General to explain to the House what went wrong. How was it possible for this man to be released? How was it possible for a dangerous sexual psychopath to be released prior to his sentence expiry?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Kelleher (Solicitor General of Canada):
subtopic: RELEASE OF PENITENTIARY INMATE WITH HISTORY OF PSYCHIATRIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly agree that what has happened here is a terrible situation. Yesterday I expressed the sympathy of all concerned to the family.
June 22, 1988

I certainly do not intend to indulge in a review of this man's record when the case is presently before the courts, and when the man has been charged. I think the Hon. Member should be much more temperate in his remarks in the House in that regard. A man is considered innocent until proven guilty, notwithstanding how abhorrent the crime may be.
The man was released on mandatory supervision, which I may remind the Hon. Member was something I have recommended be abolished in the parole reforms which I brought forward last week. I can also advise the Hon. Member that I have asked the head of Correctional Services Canada to do a complete audit on this file for me. I expect to have that by the first of the week.

Mr. Speaker, in July, 1986, Parliament was recalled in an emergency. According to the Government that emergency was to deal with dangerous offenders who were being released on mandatory supervision. Parliament passed Bill C-67. The Department of the Solicitor General had the authority to detain this man, yet he was released a year and a half before sentence expiry.
How was it possible for this man to be released? Would the Solicitor General not agree that, in the circumstances, given his record, given the fact that he had psychiatric problems dating back 30 years, his Department ought to have exercised the authority that Parliament gave to him two years ago, and detained this man?

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a short question of privilege. Earlier today, before we had that unbelievable but very warranted discussion the kind of which I had not seen in my 25 years in this House, the Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) tabled a document. I must recognize, having taken a copy in English, that it is very short. But my question, Mr. Speaker is not whether that document is very long or very short, it deals with a sacred principle in this House on which I always insist. That principle is that no document should be tabled in only one of the two official languages, especially by a Minister of the Crown.
However short, the document was tabled in English only. I object. And the reason for that is, as I have always stated in my 25 years in this place that if there is a Department that should be aware of bilingualism, it is the Department of External Affairs, which must reflect the policy of bilingualism on every occasion and in every area.
If that Department could not find the time to translate two short pages on undesirables, even though we have been knowing since yesterday the Minister would be rising today to table the document, I wonder what is going on in External Affairs. I let that go by. Mr. Speaker, this is unacceptable, and I repeat unacceptable from any Minister of the Crown, but especially from the Department of External Affairs.

speechtext: There is a tradition in this place according to which Member who has abstained may rise briefly to give an explanation. I would ask Hon. Members to extend that courtesy.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am profoundly opposed to those provisions of the Meech Lake Accord which may weaken the important role of the federal Government and allow for the possibility that fundamental rights of women and minorities as set out in the Charter may be overridden, diminish the status of the Yukon and Northwest Territories, and show a lack of recognition and respect for the aboriginal peoples of Canada. [Translation]
But at the same time, Mr. Speaker, I regretted Quebec's exclusion of the Constitutional Accord of 1981, as well as I have always favoured the recognition of Quebec's distinct society which requires, for a fundamental part of this character to be guaranteed, that the principles of Bill 101 be obeyed and applied.

For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I have abstained on this most important vote.

ALLOTTED DAYS-PRECEDENCE OF OPPOSITION MOTIONS Mr. Nelson A. Riis (Kamloops-Shuswap): Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order to suggest that this should not be an allotted day. I refer to the terms of Standing Order 58(5) and Citation 478 of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition which reads:
Under the terms of S. O. 58(5), twenty-five days are allotted to the business of Supply in each year. Although technically the business under discussion is government business, motions given precedence on these allotted days may be moved only by Members in opposition to the Government. To this extent, there is a distinction between the business of supply and other government business with respect to S. O. 18.
I submit that, as a result of today, the motion given precedence was, of course, an initiative by the Government. For that reason, I believe that today ought not to be an allotted day.
